one_liner: AST-based, extensible Rust CommonMark/GFM parser and HTML renderer, 9-14% faster than cmark on one 198 KB fixture.
what_it_does: rushdown parses CommonMark 0.31.2 (plus optional GFM extensions) into an arena-backed AST and renders HTML, by the author of Go's goldmark and modelled on it. The main API is new_markdown_to_html(parser options, renderer options, parser extension, renderer extension), which returns a reusable closure that writes into any TextWrite (String by default); markdown_to_html_string is a one-shot helper. Users can add their own AST node kinds, block and inline parsers, AST transformers and node renderers from outside the crate. It is a Rust API, not a cmark-compatible C API.
how_it_is_fast: The README names no mechanism; the source shows the usual zero-copy parser design. AST nodes live in a Vec-backed arena addressed by index (NodeRef, initial capacity 1024), text is kept as Segment/Index offsets into the source string rather than copied, and memchr drives newline, backslash and entity scanning. Autolink and table scanners are DFAs generated by re2rust (src/scanner/*.re), HTML entities use a compile-time phf map, and built-in node kinds are rendered through an enum match with optional override slots rather than dynamic dispatch. cmark itself also uses re2c scanners and a C arena, so the measured gap is small and unexplained.
when_to_use: Rust services rendering CommonMark or GFM to HTML that build one converter and call it many times (the cached row: about 3.18 ms for a 198 KB document, roughly 64 MB/s, derived from page data).
Pipelines that need to inspect or rewrite the AST (custom @mention syntax, heading IDs, link rewriting) before rendering, with goldmark-style extension points.
no_std targets with alloc: the no-std feature swaps std collections for hashbrown.
Replacing comrak or pulldown-cmark in a Rust project when CommonMark compliance and extensibility both matter (comrak 4.25 ms vs rushdown 3.34 ms on the same fixture).
when_not_to_use: C or C++ codebases: there is no C API, and the published lead over cmark is 9% like-for-like on one document, not worth an FFI layer.

Many small documents with a converter built per call: building the converter costs about 0.16 ms (3.3427 minus 3.1845 ms, derived from page data), which dwarfs parsing a 1-2 KB comment. Build it once and reuse it (it is not Send, so one per thread).
Untrusted input that relies on GFM's disallowed-raw-HTML tag filter: not supported; with allows_unsafe enabled you need a sanitizer such as ammonia (README).
Projects that need a stable API: 0.x crate with frequent breaking refactors (refactor! commits through April 2026, e.g. Emphasis split into Emphasis and Strong).
Code that builds Segment or Index values by hand from untrusted ranges: open soundness issue #2 (see gotchas).

integration.dependencies: bitflags, memchr, phf (phf_codegen at build time); hashbrown for no-std; optional pprof for profiling
integration.platforms: any Rust target; std or no_std + alloc; no architecture-specific code found beyond memchr's own SIMD
integration.thread_safety: Parser holds Rc<RefCell<ContextKeyRegistry>> and an Rc id generator, so the converter closure is neither Send nor Sync; build one per thread

gotchas: Harness flaws behind the numbers, beyond the verifier's (uninitialised 'double sum' in benches/cmark_benchmark.c, unpinned cmark master, no hardware): the single fixture benches/fixtures/data.md is the CommonMark spec text itself, about 38% of its bytes inside 708 fenced example blocks, so it is code-block heavy; the cmark C loop has no warm-up call while the goldmark driver warms up and reuses its buffer; the ftell check compares a size_t with < 0 and can never fail. None of these looks large enough to flip a 9% gap, but nothing is reproducible without a hardware and compiler record.

Rust sibling rows are not like-for-like either: rushdown runs with allows_unsafe and xhtml, comrak and markdown-rs run with their safe defaults (raw HTML omitted or escaped), and the pulldown-cmark closure also calls comrak::markdown_to_html, so its 6.0 ms row times two parsers.

Soundness: Index::str and Segment::str are safe functions that call get_unchecked on user-supplied ranges (src/text.rs; the doc comment has a '# Safety' note but the function is not marked unsafe). Issue #2 (opened 2026-08-12, with Miri output) shows UB from safe code; no maintainer reply or fix as of 2026-10-12. Normal parsing creates in-range segments, so this mostly bites extension authors.

Rendering walks the AST with a recursive ast::walk, and no nesting-depth limit was found in the parser, so pathologically deep blockquote or list nesting may exhaust the stack (cmark renders with an iterative iterator); the crate is fuzzed with cargo fuzz but this was not tested here. Defaults also differ from the benchmark: allows_unsafe and xhtml are both false unless set.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against zigmark (Zig CommonMark renderer, also measured against cmark) pick rushdown when you are in Rust and want an extensible AST with GFM extensions and a crates.io ecosystem (footnote, meta, emoji, highlighting, diagram, definition-list crates); pick zigmark for Zig. No other Markdown parser is catalogued in this category.
verified_claims_summary: The README's 'make bench' output converts the 198 KB CommonMark spec text to HTML (raw HTML allowed) in 3.34 ms with rushdown building its converter per call and 3.18 ms with a cached converter, against 3.64 ms for cmark master built Release (-O3, shared library, no LTO) and timed by a 500-iteration gettimeofday loop: 1.09x and 1.14x (derived from page data). Rust side is criterion with fat LTO, codegen-units 1 and panic=abort; CPU, OS and compiler versions are not stated.
status_note: MIT-licensed single-author 0.x crate (rushdown 0.18.0, 47 commits, 35 stars, last commit 2026-04-30) with CI on stable, beta and nightly and fuzzing; usable today, but pin the version given the breaking-change cadence and the unanswered soundness issue #2.
